info.title: Webhook Inspector API
info.description:
The public HTTP API of Webhook Inspector: create a temporary webhook endpoint, point a system under test at it, and read back every request it received — with `curl` or your own client, without the web interface.

**[Download openapi.json](/openapi.json)** — this description as a file, to import into Postman, Insomnia or Bruno or to generate a client from. Its address is `https://qa-tools.ru/openapi.json`.

To check whether Webhook Inspector is up — say, when a test that uses it fails — open https://status.qa-tools.ru: the site, the API and webhook receiving, each checked every minute from outside, with its uptime history and reports of outages.

QA Tools is a tester's personal project, written by AI agents; who runs it, who pays for it and what happens to your data are set out at https://qa-tools.ru/about.

By using the API or the MCP server, you agree to the Terms of Use at https://qa-tools.ru/terms, and the Privacy Policy at https://qa-tools.ru/privacy says what QA Tools stores and for how long.

## Quickstart

Four calls: create a session, send it a webhook, list what it captured, read one request. Then the same with a response of your own, a queue of responses for the next requests, responses by path and method, and the call that deletes a session when you are done with it.

### 1. Create a session

```bash
curl -X POST https://qa-tools.ru/api/sessions
```

```json
{
  "id": "G4t2kM8qVYp3Xn6wRz9BcH1LdF7SaJ0eU5iKcN2mQxA",
  "expiresAt": "2026-10-02T09:00:00.000Z",
  "receiveUrl": "https://hook.qa-tools.ru/s/G4t2kM8qVYp3Xn6wRz9BcH1LdF7SaJ0eU5iKcN2mQxA",
  "private": false
}
```

`id` is the session, and `receiveUrl` its webhook URL. `private` is `false`: whoever has the id has the session (see Private sessions for one that needs a key). Keep the id in a shell variable for the next calls:

```bash
SESSION=G4t2kM8qVYp3Xn6wRz9BcH1LdF7SaJ0eU5iKcN2mQxA
```

The same session is on screen, live, at `https://qa-tools.ru/v/$SESSION`.

### 2. Send a webhook

The webhook URL is `receiveUrl`, `https://hook.qa-tools.ru/s/$SESSION`: webhooks are received on a host of their own, and everything else stays on `https://qa-tools.ru`. Give it to the system under test, or call it yourself — any method, any body:

```bash
curl -X POST "https://hook.qa-tools.ru/s/$SESSION" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"event":"order.paid","orderId":42}'
```

A new session answers every request `200` with the id of the stored request, what was stored and its link in the inspector, and nothing of its body, headers or query string:

```json
{
  "ok": true,
  "requestId": "3f8a1b20-0000-4000-8000-000000000000",
  "message": "Captured by QA Tools",
  "inspectorUrl": "https://qa-tools.ru/v/G4t2kM8qVYp3Xn6wRz9BcH1LdF7SaJ0eU5iKcN2mQxA#3f8a1b20-0000-4000-8000-000000000000",
  "receivedAt": "2026-09-25T09:00:00.000Z",
  "method": "POST",
  "path": "/s/G4t2kM8qVYp3Xn6wRz9BcH1LdF7SaJ0eU5iKcN2mQxA",
  "bodySize": 35,
  "sourceIp": "203.0.113.7"
}
```

### 3. List the captured requests

```bash
curl "https://qa-tools.ru/api/sessions/$SESSION/requests"
```

Newest first, without bodies or headers:

```json
[
  {
    "id": "3f8a1b20-0000-4000-8000-000000000000",
    "method": "POST",
    "receivedAt": "2026-09-25T09:00:00.000Z",
    "bodySize": 35,
    "sourceIp": "203.0.113.7",
    "path": "/s/G4t2kM8qVYp3Xn6wRz9BcH1LdF7SaJ0eU5iKcN2mQxA",
    "response": { "state": "sent", "status": 200, "queueStep": null, "rule": null }
  }
]
```

Add `?include=headers,body` to get each request's headers and body in the same answer (at most 20 requests then), and `?order=asc&after=<id>` for only the requests that arrived after one you have already seen. Add `?wait=10` when the webhook may not have arrived yet: an answer that would be empty is held until a request arrives, for up to 10 seconds.

### 4. Read one request

```bash
REQUEST=3f8a1b20-0000-4000-8000-000000000000
curl "https://qa-tools.ru/api/sessions/$SESSION/requests/$REQUEST"
```

Everything that arrived — the headers exactly as the sender wrote them, in their order, the body, the raw request — and the response it was given. Abridged:

```json
{
  "id": "3f8a1b20-0000-4000-8000-000000000000",
  "method": "POST",
  "path": "/s/G4t2kM8qVYp3Xn6wRz9BcH1LdF7SaJ0eU5iKcN2mQxA",
  "httpVersion": "1.1",
  "queryString": "",
  "headers": [
    ["Host", "hook.qa-tools.ru"],
    ["User-Agent", "curl/8.7.1"],
    ["Accept", "*/*"],
    ["Content-Type", "application/json"],
    ["Content-Length", "35"]
  ],
  "body": "{\"event\":\"order.paid\",\"orderId\":42}",
  "bodySize": 35,
  "isBinary": false,
  "response": { "state": "sent", "status": 200, "queueStep": null, "rule": null }
}
```

### 5. Answer with a response of your own

Create the session with a `response`: a status, headers as `[name, value]` pairs, a body written as a JSON **string**, and a delay in milliseconds.

```bash
curl -X POST https://qa-tools.ru/api/sessions \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"response":{"status":201,"headers":[["x-trace-id","abc-123"]],"body":"{\"received\":true}","delayMs":500}}'
```

```json
{
  "id": "cc1cYVF7YlD2hyD1Y5EVPMgLqhXtNZYCD9rOBucvfwg",
  "expiresAt": "2026-10-02T09:00:00.000Z",
  "receiveUrl": "https://hook.qa-tools.ru/s/cc1cYVF7YlD2hyD1Y5EVPMgLqhXtNZYCD9rOBucvfwg",
  "private": false
}
```

Every webhook to it now waits half a second and gets exactly that answer:

```bash
CUSTOM=cc1cYVF7YlD2hyD1Y5EVPMgLqhXtNZYCD9rOBucvfwg
curl -i -X POST "https://hook.qa-tools.ru/s/$CUSTOM" -d 'ping'
```

```http
HTTP/1.1 201 Created
x-trace-id: abc-123
x-webhook-inspector-request-id: 1277aa3e-3050-4549-b4de-56c893bb5946
x-qa-tools-request-id: 1277aa3e-3050-4549-b4de-56c893bb5946
x-content-type-options: nosniff
content-security-policy: sandbox; default-src 'none'
content-type: application/json; charset=utf-8
content-length: 17

{"received":true}
```

(`Date` and the connection headers are left out above.)

### 6. Change the response later

A running session can be switched to the default answer, or to another custom one, without losing what it captured:

```bash
curl -X PUT "https://qa-tools.ru/api/sessions/$CUSTOM/response" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"mode":"default"}'
```

```json
{
  "response": null,
  "customResponse": {
    "status": 201,
    "headers": [["x-trace-id", "abc-123"]],
    "body": "{\"received\":true}",
    "delayMs": 500
  }
}
```

`response: null` means the session answers the default again; `customResponse` is kept, and `{"mode":"custom","response":{…}}` switches back or saves a new one.

### 7. Answer the next requests with a queue

To check how a sender retries, give the session a queue: each of the next requests gets the next step, and after the last step the session's own response answers again.

```bash
curl -X PUT "https://qa-tools.ru/api/sessions/$CUSTOM/queue" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"steps":[{"status":503,"headers":[["retry-after","1"]]},{"status":503}]}'
```

```json
{
  "response": null,
  "customResponse": {
    "status": 201,
    "headers": [["x-trace-id", "abc-123"]],
    "body": "{\"received\":true}",
    "delayMs": 500
  },
  "queue": {
    "steps": [
      { "status": 503, "headers": [["retry-after", "1"]], "body": null, "delayMs": 0 },
      { "status": 503, "headers": [], "body": null, "delayMs": 0 }
    ],
    "next": 1,
    "total": 2
  },
  "rules": []
}
```

The next two webhooks get `503`, the third the session's response, and each request's `response` names the step that answered it, `"queueStep": { "index": 2, "total": 2 }`, or `null`. `POST /api/sessions/{sessionId}/queue/restart` starts the queue again from step 1, clearing the requests does too, and `DELETE /api/sessions/{sessionId}/queue` removes it. A session can also be created with its queue, `{"response":{…},"queue":{"steps":[…]}}`.

### 8. Answer by path and method

To mock a small API on one URL, give the session rules: a request whose method and path match a rule gets that rule's response — the first rule that matches — and takes no step of the queue.

```bash
curl -X PUT "https://qa-tools.ru/api/sessions/$CUSTOM/rules" \
  -H 'Content-Type: application/json' \
  -d '{"rules":[{"method":"POST","path":"/orders","response":{"status":201,"body":"{\"id\":42}"}},{"method":null,"path":"/status/*","response":{"status":200,"body":"{\"ok\":true}"}}]}'
```

```json
{
  "response": null,
  "customResponse": {
    "status": 201,
    "headers": [["x-trace-id", "abc-123"]],
    "body": "{\"received\":true}",
    "delayMs": 500
  },
  "queue": {
    "steps": [
      { "status": 503, "headers": [["retry-after", "1"]], "body": null, "delayMs": 0 },
      { "status": 503, "headers": [], "body": null, "delayMs": 0 }
    ],
    "next": 1,
    "total": 2
  },
  "rules": [
    {
      "method": "POST",
      "path": "/orders",
      "response": { "status": 201, "headers": [], "body": "{\"id\":42}", "delayMs": 0 }
    },
    {
      "method": null,
      "path": "/status/*",
      "response": { "status": 200, "headers": [], "body": "{\"ok\":true}", "delayMs": 0 }
    }
  ]
}
```

```bash
curl -X POST "https://hook.qa-tools.ru/s/$CUSTOM/orders" -d '{"item":"book"}'
```

```json
{ "id": 42 }
```

`POST …/orders` gets rule 1's `201` and any method on `…/status/` and below rule 2's `200`; every other request — `GET …/orders`, `POST …/orders/` — gets the queue's next step, then the session's response, as before. The path is what follows `/s/{sessionId}`, compared exactly as sent, and a `*` at its end matches any rest of it. Each request's `response` names the rule that answered it, `"rule": { "index": 1 }`, or `null`. `{"rules":[]}` removes them, and a session can also be created with them, `{"rules":[…]}`.

### 9. Delete the session when you are done

```bash
curl -X DELETE "https://qa-tools.ru/api/sessions/$CUSTOM"
```

It answers `204` with no body. The session is gone at once with everything it held — its captured requests, their responses and its response settings — so a run in CI leaves nothing behind. Its webhook URL then answers `404` with `errorCode` `1001`, as for an id that never existed, and so does every call about the session, a second `DELETE` included. An expired session is not deleted: it answers `410` with `1002`, and the cleanup removes it within about 10 minutes.

A run that may be interrupted before it gets here — a test that crashes, times out or is cancelled — can create its session with a lifetime instead, `curl -X POST https://qa-tools.ru/api/sessions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"expiresInSeconds":3600}'`, and the session ends an hour later on its own (see Concepts).

## Concepts

- **The session id is the access key, unless the session is private.** There are no accounts. The 43-character id in `/s/{sessionId}` is also what reads, deletes and reconfigures a public session, so whoever has its webhook URL has the session. A private session answers only calls that present its access key (see Private sessions).
- **Two hosts.** Webhooks are received on `https://hook.qa-tools.ru` and nowhere else; `POST /api/sessions` and `GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}` give the session's webhook URL as `receiveUrl`. The API, the View page and the realtime connection are on `https://qa-tools.ru`. Since 0.36.0 `https://qa-tools.ru/s/{sessionId}` stores nothing: it answers `410` with `errorCode` `1009`, and its `message` names the webhook URL to use.
- **The View page.** `https://qa-tools.ru/v/{sessionId}` shows the same session in a browser, and new requests appear there as they arrive.
- **Lifetime: 7 days after last use.** A captured webhook, a read of the session (`GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}`), a change of its response, each call on its response queue and a save of its rules move the expiry 7 days ahead (at most once an hour), or, for a session created with an idle window, that window ahead. Listing, searching, querying, reading and deleting requests do not, and neither does reading the status of sessions (`POST /api/sessions/status`). An expired session answers `410` and cannot be revived; it is removed with everything it captured within about 10 minutes. `DELETE /api/sessions/{sessionId}` removes a session at once, with everything it captured (step 9); deleting is not a use.
- **Lifetime at creation.** `POST /api/sessions` with `expiresInSeconds`, an integer from 60 to 604800 (7 days), alone or beside `response` and `queue`, creates a session that ends that many seconds after its creation, whatever happens to it: no use moves its expiry, and `expiresAt` is that end. It only shortens a session, so a test that never reaches its clean-up step leaves nothing behind for long. Without it a session expires 7 days after its last use, as above.
- **Idle window at creation.** `POST /api/sessions` with `expiresAfterIdleSeconds`, an integer from 3600 to 604800 (1 hour to 7 days), alone or beside `response` and `queue`, creates a session that expires that long after its last use instead of 7 days: every use above moves its expiry that far ahead again, at most once an hour or, for a window under 10 hours, once a tenth of the window — 6 minutes for an hour — so a use every 10 minutes keeps a 1-hour session alive. Not together with `expiresInSeconds`: a session either slides or ends at a fixed time. `GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}` says which: `expiresAfterIdleSeconds`, the window, or `lifetimeEndsAt`, the fixed end.
- **No sender address.** `POST /api/sessions` with `{"storeSourceIp":false}`, alone or beside the other keys, creates a session whose requests keep no sender IP address: `sourceIp` is `null` in every answer about them, the default answer and the events included. The headers the sender sent are kept as sent. Set at creation only; `GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}` gives it as `storeSourceIp`.
- **The newest 1000 requests are kept.** The 1001st request removes the oldest one.
- **Payload limit: 1 MiB** (1,048,576 bytes) per request body. A larger webhook is refused `413` and not stored.
- **Search.** `POST /api/sessions/{sessionId}/requests/search` with `{"words":["48213"]}` answers, for each word, the ids of the requests whose raw request — request line, headers and body — contains it, as exact bytes: case-sensitive, no wildcards. 1 to 8 words of 3 to 200 bytes each. A search may run for 2 seconds (`503` / `1011` after that), and the server runs two at a time (`429` / `1012` for the next).
- **Many requests in one call.** `GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}/requests` takes `include=headers,body` for the headers and bodies in the same answer (at most 20 requests then), `limit` (1 to 1000), `order=asc` for oldest first, `after=<request id>` for only the requests that arrived after that one, and `since=<date-time>`. Page through everything with `order=asc&after=<the last id>&limit=100` until the answer is empty: each request comes once. `POST /api/sessions/{sessionId}/requests/query` takes the same five and filters by a header, `{"headers":[{"name":"X-Merchant-ID","value":"123"}]}` (the name in any case, the value whole), or by the bytes of the body, `{"body":["\"orderId\":42"]}`, all conditions together; the filters travel in its body, never in a URL. An unknown or repeated parameter, or an invalid value, is `400` / `1013`.
- **Wait for a webhook in one call.** `GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}/requests?wait=10` answers at once when the list it describes is not empty, and otherwise holds the answer until a request arrives for it, or for `wait` seconds, then answers `[]`. `wait` is 1 to 30. `after=<request id>` waits for anything newer than that request; without `after` the call waits for the session's first request, so `DELETE /api/sessions/{sessionId}/requests`, then trigger the webhook, then `GET …/requests?wait=10` needs no id and no clock. It combines with `include`, `limit` and `order`, not with `since`. Clearing the requests ends a wait at once with `[]`; deleting the session ends it with `404` / `1001`; a session expired when the time runs out is `410` / `1002`.
- **What is captured.** Every method except `CONNECT` — the eight OpenAPI can name are listed below, and the others are answered the same way. The path is `/s/{sessionId}`, with or without a trailing slash, or any path under it, such as `/s/{sessionId}/stripe/events`. The path and the query string are stored as sent, dot segments, doubled slashes and percent-encoding included, and so are the headers: each name in the sender's case, in the sender's order, duplicates kept, nothing added. The body bytes are stored whatever the content type, and a body that is not valid UTF-8 is returned as Base64. The webhook host speaks HTTP/1.1, so an HTTP/2 client falls back to it and `httpVersion` is `1.1`. `sourceIp` is the address the sender connected from, or `null` for a session created with `storeSourceIp: false`; a sender's own `X-Forwarded-For` is stored as a header like any other and does not change it.

## Private sessions

A private session is opened only by its access key, so its webhook URL can sit in the configuration of the system under test, in a log or in a CI report without letting whoever sees it read what the session captured. Whoever has the URL can still send it webhooks.

Create one with `"private": true`. With no `Authorization` header the server draws a key, 43 letters and digits, and answers it once, as `accessKey`: it is never shown again, and nothing can recover it.

```bash
curl -X POST https://qa-tools.ru/api/sessions -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"private":true}'
```

```json
{
  "id": "G4t2kM8qVYp3Xn6wRz9BcH1LdF7SaJ0eU5iKcN2mQxA",
  "expiresAt": "2026-10-02T09:00:00.000Z",
  "receiveUrl": "https://hook.qa-tools.ru/s/G4t2kM8qVYp3Xn6wRz9BcH1LdF7SaJ0eU5iKcN2mQxA",
  "private": true,
  "accessKey": "Rk3Xq9Lm2Vb7Nc4Hj8Wt1Pz6Fd0Sg5Ya2Ue7Io4TmNq"
}
```

- **One key for many sessions.** Keep the key with your CI's secrets and create the next sessions under it: `curl -X POST https://qa-tools.ru/api/sessions -H "Authorization: Bearer $WEBHOOK_INSPECTOR_ACCESS_KEY" -H 'Content-Type: application/json' -d '{"private":true}'` creates a private session the same key opens, and its answer carries no `accessKey`. Use a key the server drew, or 43 random letters and digits of your own: any value of that shape is taken, and it keeps working after the sessions created under it are gone. An `Authorization` header that carries no such key — another scheme, an empty `Bearer`, a value of another length or with other characters than `A-Z a-z 0-9 _ -` — is `400` / `1005`, and nothing is created.
- **Present the key on every call about the session.** `Authorization: Bearer <key>` on the API and on the MCP server `/mcp`; beside its id in `accessKeys` for `POST /api/sessions/status`, `{"ids":["<id>"],"accessKeys":{"<id>":"<key>"}}`; and on the WebSocket as the subprotocol `webhook-inspector.access-key.<key>`, offered beside `webhook-inspector` (see Realtime) — until the date the changelog's 1.19.0 entry gives, the old names `qa-tools.access-key.<key>` and `qa-tools` are taken too. Never in a URL or a query string: a key there is no key.
- **Without its key, a private session does not exist.** A call without the key, or with another, is answered exactly as for a session that does not exist: `404` with `errorCode` `1001`, `not_found` in the status read, the socket closed `4404`, the MCP tools' `1001`. An expired private session answers so too, and `410` / `1002` only with its key.
- **What stays open.** The webhook URL receives as for any session and asks for no key, so whoever has it can send the session requests and learn that it exists. QA Tools keeps only the key's SHA-256 fingerprint, never the key.
- **Set at creation only.** `GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}` gives `private`, `true` or `false`. A session cannot be made private later, and its key cannot be changed or recovered. Without `private`, or with `false`, a creation ignores `Authorization` and the session is public, as before. In the browser, the View page opens a private session once it has the key — from a link with access, `https://qa-tools.ru/v/<session-id>#key=<key>`, whose fragment no browser sends to the server, or pasted on its `Session not found` page — and keeps it in that browser; without the key, it shows the page of a session that does not exist.

## Custom response rules

- `status` is **required**: an integer from 200 to 599. `headers`, `body`, `delayMs` and `template` are optional, and any other key is refused.
- `body` is a JSON **string** that holds the exact text to answer — JSON, broken JSON, XML, HTML or plain text — such as `"{\"received\":true}"`. It must be at most 64 KiB and contain no U+0000 character (the six characters of a `\u0000` escape are text like any other), and it is sent byte for byte; no `requestId` is added to it, unless the response is a template. Leave it out, or send `null` or `""`, for no body.
- `204`, `205` and `304` take no body: a non-empty `body` with them is refused.
- `headers` is an array of `[name, value]` pairs, at most 20 and at most 8 KiB together, sent in that order, duplicates included. A name is at most 128 bytes of token characters; a value at most 1024 bytes of visible ASCII, space and tab.
- **Reserved header names** are refused, compared case-insensitively: `Content-Length`, `Content-Encoding`, `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Transfer-Encoding`, `Connection`, `Keep-Alive`, `Upgrade`, `TE`, `Trailer`, `Host`, `Set-Cookie`, `Refresh`, `Alt-Svc`, `WWW-Authenticate`, `Proxy-Authenticate`, `Clear-Site-Data`, `Strict-Transport-Security`, `Content-Security-Policy`, `Content-Security-Policy-Report-Only`, `Public-Key-Pins`, `Access-Control-Allow-Credentials`, `NEL`, `Report-To`, `Reporting-Endpoints`, `X-Webhook-Inspector-Request-Id`, and any name beginning with `X-QA-Tools-`.
- **`Location` only on a redirect:** a status from 300 to 399 may carry `Location`, and its value must begin with `/s/`: a path on the webhook host, such as `["Location","/s/<sessionId>/after"]`, never an absolute URL. Several are sent in order. `Location` with any other status, or another target, is refused. `Refresh` stays reserved on every status.
- **`Content-Type` is an ordinary header:** configure it to say what the body is, as `["Content-Type","text/plain"]`. It is sent exactly as configured, with no `charset` added, and also when there is no body. A response with a body and no configured `Content-Type` carries `Content-Type: application/json; charset=utf-8`.
- **Every answer carries `Content-Security-Policy: sandbox; default-src 'none'`**, so a browser that opens the webhook URL runs no script from it and loads nothing for it, whatever the body. It cannot be configured.
- `delayMs` is from 0 to 30000. The request is stored and shown before the delay, and the sender waits.
- **`template: true` makes `body` a template:** its placeholders are filled in from each request it answers — `{{request.id}}`, `{{request.method}}`, `{{request.path}}`, `{{request.query.<name>}}` (the first value, decoded), `{{request.header.<name>}}` (the first value, the name in any case) and `{{request.body.<path>}}` (keys of a JSON body separated by dots, a number indexing an array), such as `"{\"id\":\"{{request.id}}\",\"orderId\":\"{{request.body.order.id}}\"}"`. A value is escaped for the response's `Content-Type` — JSON without one — so a quoted placeholder stays valid JSON, and HTML or XML stays text; a missing value, `null`, an object or an array is empty; the answer stays within 64 KiB, a value that does not fit left empty. Every `{{` must start a placeholder, closed by `}}` with nothing else inside, or the response is refused. Without `template`, a body is sent as written, `{{` included. It works for a queue's steps and a rule's response too, and the MCP tools take it.
- **The response can be changed afterwards**, with `PUT /api/sessions/{sessionId}/response` (step 6). Requests already captured keep the answer they were given.
- A rule broken answers `400` with `errorCode` `1005`, and its `message` names the field.

## Response queue

A session may hold a queue of 1 to 10 responses layered over its own response, Default or Custom (step 7). Each captured request, whatever its method and path, takes the next step; after the last step every request gets the session's response again, whatever it is at that moment. A used-up queue stays saved until it is removed.

- `PUT /api/sessions/{sessionId}/queue` with `{"steps":[…]}` saves the steps and starts the queue from step 1. Each step is a whole response — `status`, `headers`, `body`, `delayMs` — checked by exactly the rules above; a step that breaks one is refused with `1005`, and the `message` names it by its place in the array, `steps[1]` for the second. 0 or more than 10 steps are refused too. The body may be up to 1 MiB, as on every call: enough for 10 steps of ordinary text at every limit. Text that JSON escapes is written larger — a quote or a backslash as two bytes, a control character as six, a non-ASCII letter as six where a serializer writes it as `\uXXXX` — and a queue over 1 MiB is refused `413`: shorten it, or send non-ASCII text unescaped. The server handles eight bodies over 128 KiB of a save or a creation at a time and refuses the next at once, `429` with `errorCode` `1017` and `Retry-After: 1` (see Limits).
- `POST /api/sessions/{sessionId}/queue/restart` starts the saved queue from step 1 again without sending it; `DELETE /api/sessions/{sessionId}/queue` removes it, and the session answers its response alone. Both take no body.
- `DELETE /api/sessions/{sessionId}/requests` starts the queue from step 1 as well. Changing the session's response and deleting one request leave it where it is.
- `POST /api/sessions` takes a queue beside `response`, `{"queue":{"steps":[…]}}`, and the session starts at step 1.
- `GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}` and the answers of the three calls carry it as `queue`: the `steps` at their effective values, `next` — the step the next request gets, or `null` once every step has answered — and `total`; `queue` is `null` for a session without one.
- Every captured request records the step that answered it: `response.queueStep` in the request list and the detail, `{"index":2,"total":7}`, or `null` when the session's response answered.
- A step's delay is waited out like the session response's: the request is stored and shown first. The steps are taken one request at a time, so concurrent requests each get a different step, in the order they were stored.

## Response rules

A session may hold up to 20 ordered **response rules** over its queue and its response (step 8): a method, or `null` for any method, a path pattern and a response. A captured request is answered by the first rule it matches, with that rule's status, headers, body and delay, and takes no step of the queue; a request no rule matches is answered as without rules — the queue's next step while it has steps left, then the session's response.

- `PUT /api/sessions/{sessionId}/rules` with `{"rules":[…]}` saves the whole ordered list, replacing every rule the session had; `{"rules":[]}` removes them all. Each rule is `{"method":"POST","path":"/orders","response":{…}}`, its `response` checked by exactly the rules above; a rule that breaks a check is refused with `1005`, and the `message` names it by its place, `rules[1].path` for the second, and quotes nothing it holds. More than 20 rules are refused too. The body may be up to 1 MiB, as on every call: enough for 20 rules of ordinary responses, or 14 at every limit; a body over 128 KiB takes one of the eight places of large bodies (see Limits).
- **The method** is one of the 34 the webhook host captures, in upper case — `CONNECT` is not one — or `null` for any. `HEAD` is a method of its own: a rule for `GET` does not answer a `HEAD`.
- **The path** is matched against what follows `/s/{sessionId}`, exactly as the request sent it: case-sensitive, nothing decoded or normalised — `/%6Frders`, `/Orders` and `/orders/` are not `/orders` — and the query string is not part of it; the session's own URL, with or without its trailing slash, is `/`. A path ending in `*` matches every path that starts with what comes before it: `/items/*` matches `/items/1` and `/items/a/b`, not `/items`. No other character is special: `%`, `_` and `.` match only themselves, and there are no regular expressions. A path starts with `/`, is at most 1024 characters of visible ASCII (`!` to `~`), holds no `?`, and holds `*` only as its last character: write any other character, a space or a letter outside ASCII, percent-encoded, as a request sends it. A request sent in absolute form, `POST http://hook.qa-tools.ru/s/{sessionId}/orders HTTP/1.1`, is captured with that whole URL as its path and matches no rule: it is answered as a request no rule matches.
- `POST /api/sessions` takes rules beside the other keys, `{"rules":[…]}`, checked after them.
- `GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}`, the answers of every call that changes a session's response, queue or rules, and `session.updated` carry them as `rules`, always an array, each rule's response at its effective values; `[]` for a session without rules.
- Every captured request records the rule that answered it: `response.rule` in the request list and the events, `{"index":2}`, and in the detail with what the rule matched on as it was then, `{"index":2,"method":"GET","path":"/status"}`; `null` when no rule answered.
- Saving the rules is a use of the session, does not move the end of a session created with a lifetime, and does not start the queue again. A request already inside its delay keeps the answer it had.

## Realtime: WebSocket `/ws/{sessionId}`

`wss://qa-tools.ru/ws/{sessionId}` announces what happens to a session while it is open. OpenAPI cannot describe it, so it is described here. It is one-directional: the server sends JSON text frames and the client sends nothing.

- `ready` — `{"type":"ready"}`, first, once the connection is subscribed. Load the request list (`GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}/requests`) at this moment, and again after every reconnection, so nothing captured in between is missed.
- `request.received` — one new request, in the shape of a row of the request list:

```json
{
  "type": "request.received",
  "data": {
    "id": "3f8a1b20-0000-4000-8000-000000000000",
    "method": "POST",
    "receivedAt": "2026-09-25T09:00:00.000Z",
    "bodySize": 35,
    "sourceIp": "203.0.113.7",
    "path": "/s/G4t2kM8qVYp3Xn6wRz9BcH1LdF7SaJ0eU5iKcN2mQxA",
    "response": { "state": "pending", "status": 200, "queueStep": null, "rule": null }
  }
}
```

More events are sent only to a connection that asks for them in its URL, `?events=` followed by comma-separated names: `response.recorded` (a request's response finished: `{"type":"response.recorded","data":{"id":"…","response":{"state":"sent","status":200,"queueStep":null,"rule":null}}}`), `request.deleted` (one request was deleted: `{"type":"request.deleted","data":{"id":"…"}}`), `requests.cleared` (every request was deleted: `{"type":"requests.cleared"}`) and `session.updated` (the response changed, the response queue was saved, restarted or removed — a restart or a removal without a queue publishes nothing — or the rules were saved: `data` holds `response`, `customResponse`, `queue` and `rules`, the same fields `GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}` returns). A request that takes a step of the queue publishes no `session.updated`: its `request.received` names the step, `queueStep`, from which the queue's `next` follows, and `requests.cleared` means the queue starts again from step 1. Every viewer receives them, the one that made the change included, and none is replayed: a connection that was down catches up by reloading on its next `ready`. A session's events arrive in the order the calls that caused them took effect, so a client that applies each as it arrives ends where the server is. For example `wss://qa-tools.ru/ws/{sessionId}?events=response.recorded`. Unknown names are ignored.

An unknown session is refused with close code `4404`, an expired one with `4410`, and an open connection is closed with `4404` when its session is deleted; do not reconnect after any of these. One address may have **16 connections open at a time**, an IPv6 address counted by its `/64`: the 17th is refused before it opens, `429` with `errorCode` `1020` and `Retry-After: 1`, which a browser sees as a failed connection (`1006`) — reconnect after a delay, as after any interruption, and it gets in once another connection of the address has closed. An open connection stays open when its session expires. Any other close is an interruption: reconnect. The server pings every 30 seconds, and cuts a connection that falls more than 4 MiB of events behind, a client that has stopped reading; that close is an interruption too. So is a close by a server that may have missed an event — it cuts every connection it holds — and `1013`, Try Again Later, before `ready`, from a server not yet reading its realtime channel: reconnect, and the list loaded on the next `ready` holds whatever arrived meanwhile.

A private session's connection presents its access key as a subprotocol of the handshake, beside `webhook-inspector`: `new WebSocket('wss://qa-tools.ru/ws/{sessionId}', ['webhook-inspector', 'webhook-inspector.access-key.' + key])`. The server answers the first subprotocol offered that carries no key, `webhook-inspector` here, and never echoes the key; without the key, or with another, the connection is closed `4404`, as for an unknown session. A public session needs neither. Until the date the changelog's 1.19.0 entry gives, the old names are taken too, alone or beside the new: `qa-tools`, and the key as `qa-tools.access-key.<key>`; offered under both prefixes, the key must be the same.

An API test without a browser does not need the socket to wait for a webhook: `GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}/requests?wait=10` waits in one ordinary call and answers with the request itself (see Concepts).

## Limits

Each address may create **60 sessions a minute** and make **1200 other API calls a minute**. The two are counted apart, so creating sessions uses none of the 1200, and an IPv6 address counts by its `/64`. The minute starts with the first call counted in it.

Every answer of an API route, errors included, tells you where you stand:

- `X-RateLimit-Limit` — the calls of this kind allowed in a minute, `60` or `1200`;
- `X-RateLimit-Remaining` — how many are left after this one;
- `X-RateLimit-Reset` — the seconds until the minute ends and the count starts again.

A call over a limit is answered `429` with `errorCode` `1015` and `Retry-After` in seconds, and nothing is done.

An address may also have **128 calls in flight** at a time, on the API and the MCP server together, waits included: a call is in flight from the moment its request line and headers arrive until its answer has been written, or its client has gone, and the server has finished with it. The 129th is refused at once, before its body is read: `429`, `errorCode` `1019`, `Retry-After: 1`, and nothing is done. A CI run with 100 waits pending still has room for its other calls. A call refused `1015` takes none unless its body is drained: on a connection the server is about to close (`Connection: close`, or HTTP/1.0), a refusal before the body reads and discards a declared body of up to 4 MiB first, so that the answer is not lost to a reset, and that drain holds a place until the answer is written; the 129th, holding none, is answered at once and never drained. An answer written before the server has read the request's whole body ends the connection, `Connection: close`, on a connection kept alive too: it can be lost to a reset on a client still sending, and the next call goes on a new connection. In practice such an answer leaves the connection alive only for a body of up to about 100 KB sent with its headers, or none; a larger one ends it even when sent whole. A call whose body the server reads, as it does before answering any call it accepts, keeps the connection alive whatever the body's size, except a `413` (`1004`) for a body over its limit and a `400` (`1006`) for one that is not UTF-8, or not JSON on a route that takes no body, which always close the connection.

The answers not yet written are bounded too, on the API and the MCP server together: **16 MiB from one address and 64 MiB on the server**, an IPv6 address counted by its `/64`, an answer counting its body's bytes from the moment it is ready until it has been written whole, or its client has gone. An answer that would pass either while another answer of its address is still being written is not sent: its call is answered `429`, `errorCode` `1019`, `Retry-After: 1`, in place of the answer. The call itself has been carried out — a session it created exists, a change it made is saved — so calling it again repeats it, and a creation called again creates another session. An address's first answer is always sent, whatever its size; an answer with an error status is never refused this way; and a `HEAD`, a list with `include`, which is streamed, and a call still waiting count nothing. An answer counts only while it is being written, so a client that reads each answer as it comes meets this bound only when its address has more than 16 MiB of answers being written at once — many large reads in parallel on a slow link, or many clients behind one shared address — or the server more than 64 MiB.

The server writes **four lists with bodies** at a time — `include` holding `body`, on `GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}/requests` or `POST /api/sessions/{sessionId}/requests/query` — and refuses the next at once: `429`, `errorCode` `1016`, `Retry-After: 1`. Lists with headers alone or without `include` are never refused this way, and a call waiting with `wait` takes its place only once it has requests to write. Searches, and queries with a `body` condition, keep their own two at a time; queries with header conditions alone, or none, have two more of their own. The next of either is refused at once: `429`, `errorCode` `1012`, `Retry-After: 1`.

It also handles **eight large bodies** at a time — a body over 128 KiB, or sent chunked, of `POST /api/sessions`, `PUT /api/sessions/{sessionId}/response`, `PUT /api/sessions/{sessionId}/queue`, `PUT /api/sessions/{sessionId}/rules`, `POST /api/sessions/status`, `POST /api/sessions/{sessionId}/requests/search`, `POST /api/sessions/{sessionId}/requests/query` or a `POST` to the MCP server — and refuses the next at once, before its body is read: `429`, `errorCode` `1017`, `Retry-After: 1`. A creation with no body, a response at every limit (about 72 KiB), a few steps or rules of ordinary text, 50 session ids, 8 search words and 8 conditions are all smaller, and never refused this way unless sent chunked.

A request to `https://qa-tools.ru` carries at most **100 header lines**, `Host` among them; one with more is refused `431` before it reaches the API, with no `errorCode`. Webhooks to the webhook host have no such limit.

Webhooks to `https://hook.qa-tools.ru` are not counted per minute: every one within the limits is captured. They are received within a budget of memory instead, **64 MiB at a time, 16 MiB of it from one address**: a webhook counts its declared body, at most 1 MiB, plus 16 KiB, 256 bytes a header line and 64 KiB for its answer, from the moment its headers arrive until its answer has been written. One that does not fit waits, first come first served, before its body is read, and is captured as soon as there is room, so a burst of large webhooks from one sender is captured at the pace the server stores them while other senders' webhooks still go in. The webhooks waiting for room are bounded too, each counted by its headers, 16 KiB and 256 bytes a header line: at most 64 MiB of them may wait on the server, plus the first waiting webhook of each address, and 16 MiB of them from one address. A webhook that has waited 30 seconds for room is refused `503` with `errorCode` `1018` and `Retry-After: 1`, and nothing is stored. One that must wait while another webhook from its address is already waiting, and does not fit the waiting line, is refused the same way **at once**, its connection closed: once the webhooks waiting from your address fill their 16 MiB, or those of every address the server's 64 MiB, every webhook of yours that has to wait behind one of yours is refused at once, however small, until there is room again. Only the first webhook of an address to wait always waits, so the largest webhook you can send is never refused for its own size. From one address alone, 512 webhooks waiting at once with up to 64 header lines each fit in its 16 MiB; with more header lines fewer do — 399 with 100 lines each. The server was measured surviving floods of waiting webhooks from 4 addresses at once with no restart. The number of attacking addresses it is stated to hold against is 4, the smallest measured: floods of pipelined requests down every connection an address may open and of large API answers that their clients leave unread were each survived from 4 addresses and ran out of memory from 8, the API answers in one run of two, measured again for 1.14.1. Connections that each wait for header lines while sending a head of 256,000 bytes, which set that number at 3 from 1.0.8, inferred from the measurement for 1.0.4, were measured for 1.14.1 surviving from 8 addresses at once, the server keeping less of each such connection. A flood of connections that each stop after the most header lines allowed, which set that number at 1 before 1.0.4, it was measured surviving from 8 addresses at once with no restart; a flood of large API answers that their clients leave unread, which set it at 1 before 1.0.8, from 4, measured without the proxy in front, and from 8 it ran out of memory. A flood pipelining many tiny requests down 256 connections from each address it was measured surviving from 8 addresses at once with no restart, and down all the 512 connections an address may open from 4; from 8 such addresses it ran out of memory. Not every kind of flood is bounded yet.

The connections themselves are bounded per address too. One address may have **512 connections open at a time to `https://hook.qa-tools.ru`**, an IPv6 address counted by its `/64`, from the moment a connection reaches the server until it closes, an idle kept-alive one included. The 513th is closed at once with no HTTP answer, the connection ended by the server, and nothing is stored; send fewer at a time, or reuse kept-alive connections, and send it again. On one connection the server reads at most **32 requests ahead of their answers**: webhooks you pipeline past them, sending one before the answer to the one before, wait in the connection, unread, until earlier ones are answered, and every one is still captured and answered in order; nothing is refused for it. Of the header lines it has read of requests still arriving — each line from its first byte until the empty line that ends its head, or a chunked body's trailers, and the rest of a connection that closes — the server holds at most **32,768 from one address** and 524,288 in all, an IPv6 address counted by its `/64`: a connection whose next line does not fit waits, unread, until lines are given back, and every webhook is still captured whole; nothing is refused for it, and the first connection of an address holding no lines, and the address's oldest, are never held by its number, so a webhook with the most header lines allowed is never held by its own size. And one address may have **16 WebSocket connections open at a time** to `wss://qa-tools.ru/ws/{sessionId}`, an IPv6 address counted by its `/64`: the 17th is refused before it opens, `429` with `errorCode` `1020` and `Retry-After: 1`.

Since 0.57.1 an answer written before the server has read the request's whole body ends the connection, `Connection: close`, on both hosts and whatever the answer, as it did on the API before: a webhook refused `503` after waiting, a `404` for an unknown path, the old webhook address's `410` and a refused WebSocket among them. A body that arrived whole, or none, keeps the connection alive.

## Forward to a local service

A provider calls only a public URL, while the service you are testing may run on your laptop or behind a VPN. `webhook-inspector-relay.mjs` is a script of one file that you run next to that service: from the moment it starts, every request the session captures is sent again to a base URL you name, with one line printed per request, until you stop it with Ctrl+C. Each request still appears on the View page and in the API as usual.

Download it, check it and read it, then run it with Node.js 22 or later, which is all it needs. Never pipe it into `node`:

```bash
curl -fO https://webhook.qa-tools.ru/webhook-inspector-relay.mjs
echo '38761689bf1581cbc2a8037b0f511d990171e8ff1d92dd8a772c9c12a411a8ae  webhook-inspector-relay.mjs' | shasum -a 256 -c    # on Linux: sha256sum -c
node webhook-inspector-relay.mjs "$SESSION" http://localhost:3000
```

```text
14:03:07 POST /stripe/events?x=1 -> 200
14:03:09 POST /stripe/events -> error: connect ECONNREFUSED 127.0.0.1:3000
```

- **Its SHA-256** is `38761689bf1581cbc2a8037b0f511d990171e8ff1d92dd8a772c9c12a411a8ae`. It changes whenever the file does, and this page always gives the one the site serves.
- **Its old name.** Until 1.16.0 the script was `qa-tools-relay.mjs`, from `https://qa-tools.ru`. Since 1.19.0 that name serves the same file, with the same SHA-256, as `webhook-inspector-relay.mjs`, reading `https://webhook.qa-tools.ru` by default, on both hosts: until the date the changelog's 1.19.0 entry gives, and on `https://qa-tools.ru` until the date its 1.16.0 entry gives, https://qa-tools.ru/changelog, which says what happens to it then. Before 1.19.0 it served the script as it was, reading `https://qa-tools.ru` by default.
- **The arguments.** The first is the session id or its webhook URL, `https://hook.qa-tools.ru/s/{sessionId}`. The second is an `http:` or `https:` base URL, such as `http://localhost:3000` or `https://staging.internal/hooks`, to which the path after `/s/{sessionId}` and the query string are added: a webhook sent to `https://hook.qa-tools.ru/s/{sessionId}/stripe/events?x=1` reaches `http://localhost:3000/stripe/events?x=1`. Requests captured before the relay starts are skipped; `--from-start` sends the ones the session holds first, oldest first. It reads the session from `https://webhook.qa-tools.ru`; `--api <base URL>` reads it from another QA Tools API, such as a local one.
- **What is sent.** One request at a time, in the order captured, each with 30 seconds to be answered: the method as captured; the headers in the order and letter case they arrived, duplicates kept, less `Host` and `Content-Length`, which are set for your service and the body sent, the connection's own headers, the eleven forwarding headers of a proxy (`X-Forwarded-*`, `X-Real-Ip`) and an `Accept-Encoding: gzip`; and the body byte for byte, binary included.
- **A relay, not a tunnel.** The sender receives the session's configured response at once, as for any webhook, not your service's: your service's status is in the relay's line and nowhere else.
- **A private session.** Set its access key in the environment variable `WEBHOOK_INSPECTOR_ACCESS_KEY`, as a CI sets a secret — or, until the date the changelog's 1.19.0 entry gives, in its old name `QA_TOOLS_ACCESS_KEY`, read when the new one is not set, with a line saying so; when both are set, the new one is read: the relay sends it as `Authorization: Bearer` on every API call, never to your service, and prints it in no line. With `--api`, the key goes to that API as well: give it an `https:` address, or `http:` only for a QA Tools running on your own machine. Unset, it reads a public session as before; set to anything but a key, empty included, it prints the usage and exits with status 2 before any call. It reads the key from the environment only, never from an argument, so the key stays out of your shell history and the process list.
- **The session id is an argument**, so it lands in your shell history; a public session's id is its access key.
- **Its calls do not keep the session alive.** It reads the session with `GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}/requests` and its `wait`, and each request with `GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}/requests/{requestId}`, which are not a use. The webhooks it relays keep the session alive as always; a session unused for its idle window, 7 days unless it was created with a shorter one, expires, and the relay then stops.
- **Its calls count toward your address's 1200 API calls a minute** (Limits above). While nothing arrives it makes one waiting call every 30 seconds, two a minute; while it sends, one call per request plus one per list answer of up to 100 requests, at most two per request. So only webhooks arriving one by one faster than about 600 a minute, or other API clients at the same address, bring it to the limit; it then prints `API rate limit reached (429, errorCode 1015)`, waits the `Retry-After` and sends the rest late, in order.
- **When something fails.** A service that cannot be reached or does not answer within 30 seconds gets an error line, and the next request is still sent. An API that cannot be reached or answers `5xx` gets an error line and is tried again after 1 second, then up to every 15 seconds; a `429` is waited out for its `Retry-After`. A session that is not found or has expired ends the relay with exit status 1, and an invalid argument prints the usage and exits with status 2.

## Errors

Every error the API answers is `{ "errorCode": …, "message": "…" }`, and a `1005` that names a place in the request body also carries `field`, the refused place in the notation its message begins with, such as `rules[1].path`. Branch on `errorCode`, which never changes meaning, and find the refused value by `field`; `message` is for people and its wording may change.

| errorCode | Name | HTTP | What to do |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `1000` | `ROUTE_NOT_FOUND` | `404` | Check the path: nothing is served there. The webhook URL is `https://hook.qa-tools.ru/s/{sessionId}` or any path under it, where a wrong session id answers `1001` instead; that host serves nothing else. |
| `1001` | `SESSION_NOT_FOUND` | `404` | The id is mistyped, the session was deleted or removed after it expired, or it is private and the call did not present its access key, or presented another. Send a private session's key; otherwise create a new session. |
| `1002` | `SESSION_EXPIRED` | `410` | The session was unused for its idle window, 7 days unless it was created with `expiresAfterIdleSeconds`, or the lifetime it was created with has passed. Create a new one; an expired session cannot be revived. |
| `1003` | `REQUEST_NOT_FOUND` | `404` | The request was deleted, pushed out by the newest 1000, belongs to another session, or the id is wrong — also when `after` names it. List the requests again. |
| `1004` | `PAYLOAD_TOO_LARGE` | `413` | The body is over 1 MiB. Send a smaller one; nothing was stored. |
| `1005` | `INVALID_RESPONSE_CONFIG` | `400` | A custom response, a step of a response queue or a response rule breaks a rule above, a queue has no steps or more than 10, the rules are more than 20 or one's method or path is refused, or `expiresInSeconds` is not an integer from 60 to 604800, `expiresAfterIdleSeconds` is not one from 3600 to 604800, or both are given, or `storeSourceIp` or `private` is not `true` or `false`, or a creation with `private` set to `true` carries an `Authorization` header that holds no access key, in which case nothing is created. Its `message` names the field, and the step or the rule by its place, `steps[1]`, `rules[1]`, and quotes nothing of the header; `field` names the same place, `rules[1].path` — none for a key the body itself may not hold or for the header. |
| `1006` | `MALFORMED_REQUEST_BODY` | `400` | A body declared JSON is empty or does not parse — or, when creating a session, changing its response, setting its response queue or its rules, searching or querying its requests, or reading the status of sessions, is not a JSON object. Send valid JSON, or no body to the calls that take none. |
| `1007` | `UNSUPPORTED_MEDIA_TYPE` | `415` | Declare `Content-Type: application/json` when creating a session with a body, whatever keys it carries, changing its response, setting its response queue or its rules, searching or querying the requests, or reading the status of sessions. A default session is created with no body and no `Content-Type` at all, and the `DELETE` calls take no body. The webhook URL never answers this: it captures any content type. |
| `1008` | `MISSING_REQUEST_CONTENT` | `400` | Only a `QUERY` sent outside `/s/`: it needs a `Content-Type` header and content (RFC 10008), and `message` names the part that is missing. Nothing was stored. The webhook URL captures such a `QUERY` instead. |
| `1009` | `RECEIVE_URL_MOVED` | `410` | The webhook was sent to `https://qa-tools.ru/s/…`, which stopped receiving webhooks in 0.36.0. Send it to the session's `receiveUrl`, `https://hook.qa-tools.ru/s/{sessionId}`, which `message` names. Nothing was stored. |
| `1010` | `INVALID_SEARCH_WORDS` | `400` | A search needs `words`: an array of 1 to 8 strings, each 3 to 200 bytes in UTF-8, and no other key. Its `message` names the rule. |
| `1011` | `SEARCH_TIMED_OUT` | `503` | The search or the query ran for 2 seconds and was cancelled: the session holds too much to read in that time. Search for fewer words, or delete requests you no longer need. |
| `1012` | `SEARCH_BUSY` | `429` | Two searches, or queries of requests with a `body` condition, were already running on the server; or, for a query with header conditions alone or none, two such queries were. Call again after `Retry-After`, one second. |
| `1013` | `INVALID_LIST_QUERY` | `400` | A parameter of the request list, or a field of a query, breaks a rule: an unknown or repeated parameter, an unknown key, `limit` outside 1 to 1000 (1 to 20 with bodies), `since` without a zone, `after` with `since`, `wait` outside 1 to 30 or with `since`, more than 8 conditions. Its `message` names the parameter or the field. |
| `1014` | `INVALID_SESSION_IDS` | `400` | A status read needs `ids`: an array of 1 to 50 distinct session ids, and no other key than `accessKeys`, which is optional; an `accessKeys` that is not an object mapping ids from `ids` to access keys is refused too. Its `message` names the rule and never quotes an id or a key. |
| `1015` | `RATE_LIMIT_EXCEEDED` | `429` | This address created 60 sessions, or made 1200 other API calls, within the minute. Nothing was done. Call again after `Retry-After` seconds; `X-RateLimit-Remaining` and `X-RateLimit-Reset` in every answer tell you where you stand. |
| `1016` | `LIST_BODIES_BUSY` | `429` | Four lists with bodies were already being written on the server. Call again after `Retry-After`, one second, or leave `body` out of `include` and read the bodies you need one by one. |

| `1018` | `CAPTURES_BUSY` | `503` | A webhook found no room among the webhooks being received — 64 MiB on the server, 16 MiB from one address — and was not stored: after it waited 30 seconds, or at once, its connection closed, when another from its address was already waiting and the webhooks waiting fill the line. Send it again after `Retry-After`, one second. |

Call again after `Retry-After`, one second, or once one of your calls has been answered. |

A request the HTTP parser itself cannot read — broken framing, headers over 16 KiB or, on `https://qa-tools.ru`, over 100 lines — is answered `400`, `431` or `408` with no `errorCode`: fall back to the HTTP status when `errorCode` is missing.

## Network

For a CI runner or a network that may reach only the addresses on an allow-list:

- **One address: `80.87.198.166`.** `qa-tools.ru` and `webhook.qa-tools.ru` — each the site, the API, the WebSocket and the MCP server, the same on both — and `hook.qa-tools.ru`, which receives webhooks, all answer on it.
- **Moving to `webhook.qa-tools.ru`.** Since 1.16.0 the site, the API, the WebSocket and the MCP server answer on `https://webhook.qa-tools.ru` too, the address they keep. The ones on `qa-tools.ru` keep working until the date the changelog's 1.16.0 entry gives, https://qa-tools.ru/changelog, which says what changes then. Webhooks stay on `hook.qa-tools.ru`.
- **HTTPS on TCP port 443.** Port 80 only redirects plain HTTP to HTTPS, with a `301`.
- **IPv4 only.** No host has an IPv6 address.
- **No CDN or proxy service in front.** Your systems connect to this address itself, so it is the only one to allow.
- **Outgoing connections only.** Webhook Inspector sends no requests to your systems: webhooks, API calls, the WebSocket and the MCP server are all connections your side opens. Allow outgoing connections to `80.87.198.166` on port 443; nothing needs letting in. The relay script runs on your machine and only reads from the API, so what it sends to your service comes from your machine, not from this address.
- **A change of address is announced at least 14 days ahead**, in this section — the new address and the day of the switch — and in an entry of the changelog, https://qa-tools.ru/changelog. The one exception is emergency recovery after losing the server: the new address is then announced in both places as soon as it is known.

## Security

**No accounts.** Anyone who has the URL of a public session can read everything it captured, delete it, change its response, its response queue and its rules, and delete the session itself: share it only with the systems that should use it. A private session is opened only by its access key (see Private sessions), sent in the `Authorization` header, never in a URL, so its URL only sends it webhooks. Keep the key as any secret: whoever has it has every session created under it.

**Do not send production secrets**, personal data or real credentials to a session. It is a testing tool: captured requests are stored as received until they or their session are deleted, or until the session expires and is removed.

`Test Request` on this page sends real requests to the API and creates real sessions, which expire like any other. It sends them to the host of this page, so for the webhook operations it shows the `410` / `1009` of `https://qa-tools.ru/s/…`: send webhooks to the webhook host with curl or your own client. The API sends no CORS headers. What it limits, and how an answer says so, is under Limits above.

## Stability

- `errorCode` values never change meaning; new ones may be added.
- Fields and endpoints may be added at any time, so ignore fields you do not know.
- A breaking change ships with a version bump and is marked **Breaking** in its entry of the changelog, https://qa-tools.ru/changelog (as text for scripts: https://qa-tools.ru/changelog.md). Entries before 1.0.0 marked a breaking change with no fixed notice period: the mark was the notice. A change of the address Webhook Inspector answers on has a notice of its own, under Network above.
- `info.version`, shown at the top of this page, is the product version that serves this description.

Subscribe with a feed reader, Slack or a Telegram bot: all changes, https://qa-tools.ru/changelog.xml · breaking changes and deprecations only, https://qa-tools.ru/changelog-breaking.xml.

Since 1.0.0 the API is under this policy:

- **Version 1, no prefix.** The API's paths stay `/api/…` and are version 1; no `/v1` prefix is added. If one endpoint ever needs an incompatible redesign, a `/api/v2/…` path appears beside it for that endpoint alone.
- **What it binds.** The promise covers the HTTP API, the webhook URLs and what they answer, the MCP server and the relay script. The web interface, its design and its texts are not bound.
- **Additions need no notice.** Fields, endpoints, optional parameters, `errorCode`s and looser limits ship at once; a client ignores fields it does not know. From 2026-11-24, a new value of an enum in an answer or an event, such as a response's `state`, ships at once too; a client accepts a value it does not know.
- **Changing what exists.** The new ships beside the old, and the old is marked deprecated with a removal date at least 30 days after the announcement and its replacement; it is removed on or after that date, or never when keeping it costs nothing. Every breaking change to a stable part gets this notice, however little it is used. The changelog announces it in a paragraph that starts **Deprecated:**, naming what is deprecated, its replacement and its removal date.
- **What cannot sit side by side**, such as a stricter limit or a changed meaning, is announced at least 30 days ahead and ships after, preferably gathered into a major release.
- **Emergencies.** A change needed for security, against abuse or overload, or to recover from an outage may ship at once; it is announced when it ships, in its changelog entry, with the reason.
- **Experimental parts.** A new part of the API may be marked experimental and change without notice until it is declared stable; a path of the OpenAPI description marked so carries `x-stability-level: experimental`. The MCP server is experimental; everything else is stable.

post.description:
Creates an anonymous session and its webhook URL, `https://hook.qa-tools.ru/s/{id}`, returned as `receiveUrl`. The session expires 7 days after its last use, or, created with `expiresAfterIdleSeconds`, that many seconds after its last use, or, created with `expiresInSeconds`, that many seconds after its creation.

**Default session:** send **no body and no `Content-Type` header at all** (`curl -X POST https://qa-tools.ru/api/sessions`). A JSON object without a `response` key, `{}` included, also creates a default session.

**Custom session:** send `Content-Type: application/json` with a `response` object.

**Response queue:** add `queue`, `{"steps":[…]}`, beside `response` or alone, and the session starts with it at step 1.

**Lifetime:** add `expiresInSeconds`, an integer from 60 to 604800, alone or beside `response` and `queue`, and the session ends that many seconds after its creation, whatever happens to it: no use moves its expiry, and `expiresAt` is that end. `{"expiresInSeconds":3600}` alone creates a default session that ends an hour later. A JSON number equal to an integer, such as `6e2`, is taken; a string, `null`, a fraction or a number outside the range is `400` / `1005`, and nothing is created.

**Idle window:** add `expiresAfterIdleSeconds`, an integer from 3600 to 604800, alone or beside `response` and `queue`, and the session expires that many seconds after its last use instead of 7 days: every use moves its expiry a full window ahead, at most once an hour, or once a tenth of a window under 10 hours. `{"expiresAfterIdleSeconds":3600}` creates a default session that expires an hour after its last use; a use every 10 minutes keeps it alive. It is taken and refused as `expiresInSeconds` is, from 3600; given together with `expiresInSeconds` it is `400` / `1005`, and nothing is created.

**Sender address:** add `"storeSourceIp": false`, alone or beside the other keys, and the session stores no sender address: every request it captures has `sourceIp` `null` — in the list, the detail, the events, the default answer and the MCP tools — and `GET` gives `storeSourceIp: false`. The headers the sender sent, `X-Forwarded-For` included, are kept as sent. `true`, or the key left out, keeps the address as every session does. Set at creation only. Only the JSON booleans are taken: `"false"`, `0`, `null`, an array or an object is `400` / `1005`, and nothing is created.

**Private session:** add `"private": true`, alone or beside the other keys, and the session answers only calls that present its access key as `Authorization: Bearer <key>`; to any other it is a session that does not exist, `404` / `1001`. With no `Authorization` header the server draws the key, 43 letters and digits, and answers it this once as `accessKey`. With `Authorization: Bearer <key>`, a key of that shape you keep — one the server drew before, or 43 random letters and digits of your own — the session is created under it, so one key opens every session created with it, and the answer carries no `accessKey`. An `Authorization` that carries no key — another scheme, an empty `Bearer`, a value of another length or other characters — is `400` / `1005`, checked after every rule of the body, and nothing is created. Without `private`, or with `false`, `Authorization` is ignored. `GET` gives `private`. Set at creation only.

At most 60 per minute per address: the 61st is `429` / `1015` with `Retry-After`, before anything else is checked, and creates nothing. Creation counts toward that limit alone, not toward the 1200 other calls. A body over 128 KiB, or sent chunked, is read only while fewer than eight such bodies of a creation, a response change, a queue save, a status read, a search or a query are being handled on the server: otherwise it is `429` / `1017` with `Retry-After: 1`, at once, after the media type and before the body is read. A body declared over 1 MiB is `413` regardless. A creation with no body, or with a response or a few steps of ordinary text, is smaller and never meets it.

After the limit, the checks run in this order, and the first that fails is the answer: media type (`415` / `1007` for anything not exactly one `application/json`, except the bodyless default create), size (`413` / `1004` over 1 MiB, which holds a response and a full queue of ordinary text), body shape (`400` / `1006` for an empty, unparseable or non-object body), configuration (`400` / `1005`: the response, then the queue, then `expiresInSeconds`, then `expiresAfterIdleSeconds`, then the two together, then `storeSourceIp`, then `rules`, then `private`, then any unknown key), then, for a private creation, its `Authorization` (`400` / `1005` when it carries no key).

post.description:
For each of up to 50 session ids, whether the session is `active`, `expired` or `not_found`, and for an active one what a list of sessions shows of it: its webhook URL, how many requests it holds, when the newest arrived and when the session was last used. The web interface's home page reads the sessions it keeps in the browser with it.

**It does not use the sessions:** no expiry moves, unlike `GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}`, so a list can be shown without keeping every session in it alive. `lastUsedAt` is the expiry minus the session's idle window, 7 days or the `expiresAfterIdleSeconds` it was created with; a use moves the expiry at most once an hour, or once a tenth of a window under 10 hours, so it may be up to that much behind the last use. For a session created with `expiresInSeconds`, whose expiry no use moves, it is the later of its creation and its newest request.

The ids travel in the body, never in the URL, and so do the access keys of private sessions: a private session is reported only with its key beside its id in `accessKeys`, `{"ids":["<id>"],"accessKeys":{"<id>":"<key>"}}`, and is otherwise `not_found`, expired or not. The `Authorization` header plays no part here, since one call asks about many sessions. An id that names no session — never created, deleted, or removed after it expired — is `not_found`, and the answer does not tell those apart.

The body is checked completely before anything is read, in this order: media type (`415` / `1007` for anything not exactly one `application/json`), size (`413` / `1004`), body shape (`400` / `1006`), the ids (`400` / `1014` for none, more than 50, one that is not a session id, one given twice, then an `accessKeys` that is not an object mapping ids among `ids` to keys of 43 characters of `A-Z a-z 0-9 _ -`, then any key other than `ids` and `accessKeys`, whose message is `The request body may contain no key other than "ids" and "accessKeys"`). `GET` and `DELETE` on this path read `status` as a session id that cannot be one: `404` / `1001`.

Once the media type is settled, and before the body is read, a body over 128 KiB or sent chunked takes one of eight places the server keeps for such bodies of a creation, a response change, a queue save, a rules save, a status read, a search or a query, until its answer ends; with all eight taken it is `429` / `1017` with `Retry-After: 1`, at once and before it is read. Fifty ids are at most about 13 KiB, even escaped, and never wait for one unless sent chunked.

put.description:
Saves up to 20 response rules, in the order they are matched, replacing every rule the session had; `{"rules":[]}` removes them all. A captured request whose method and path match a rule gets that rule's response — status, headers, body and delay — and takes no step of the response queue, whose position stays where it was; the first matching rule answers. get.description:
Newest first, at most 1000 (a session keeps its newest 1000). Without a parameter, metadata only: no bodies and no full headers.

The parameters narrow, cap, reverse and add to the list. None of them carries captured data, so they travel in the URL; to filter by a header or by the body, use `POST /api/sessions/{sessionId}/requests/query`, which takes all of them but `wait` in its body. An unknown or repeated parameter, or an invalid value, is `400` / `1013`, and its message names the parameter.

Paging: `order=asc&after=<the last id of the previous page>&limit=N`, until the answer is empty, returns every request once, in the order they arrived.

Waiting: with `wait=N`, an answer that would be empty is held until a request arrives for it, then answered; after `N` seconds with nothing, it is `[]`. With `after`, the call waits for anything newer than that request, which is resolved once, when the call arrives: deleting it meanwhile does not end the wait. Without `after`, it answers at once when the session holds any request and otherwise waits for the first. No capture is missed: a request stored after the call arrived ends the wait, and several stored together may come in one answer, as `limit` and `order` choose. Clearing the session's requests ends the wait at once with `[]`, after which the request `after` named no longer exists: wait again without `after`. Deleting the session ends it at once with `404` / `1001`; when the time runs out on a session expired by then, the answer is `410` / `1002`, and on one gone by then `404` / `1001`. A shutdown of the server answers every pending wait at once, as if its time had run out, and so does a server that loses its realtime channel for a moment, which also answers a wait it receives before it reads that channel again at its first read; call again, with `after`, and nothing is missed.

The checks, in order: the parameters (`400` / `1013`), `wait` with `since` among them; a session id that cannot be one (`404` / `1001`) and an `after` that cannot be a request id (`404` / `1003`); with `body` in `include`, four lists with bodies already being written on the server (`429` / `1016`, at once, before the list is read — with `wait`, once the call has requests to write, never while it waits); the session (`404` / `1001`, `410` / `1002`); an `after` that names no request of the session (`404` / `1003`). Does not move the expiry.

/s/{sessionId}.description:
Give this URL — the session's `receiveUrl`, `https://hook.qa-tools.ru/s/{sessionId}` — to the system under test. Every request to it is captured, stored and shown live in the session's inspector at `https://qa-tools.ru/v/{sessionId}`.

**Host.** Webhooks are received on `https://hook.qa-tools.ru`, which serves `/s/` and nothing else: any other path there answers `404` / `1000`. The same path on `https://qa-tools.ru` stopped receiving in 0.36.0: whatever the method and the path under `/s/`, it stores nothing and answers `410` / `1009 RECEIVE_URL_MOVED`, with a `message` naming the URL to use; only a path with a malformed percent-escape such as `%zz` is refused there first, by the proxy, with `400` and no `errorCode`. `Test Request` on this page goes to the page's own host and so shows that `410`.

**Methods.** The receiver accepts every method in Node's `http.METHODS` except `CONNECT` — 34 names. OpenAPI 3.1 can describe eight of them, listed below; the other 26 are accepted and answered exactly the same way: `QUERY`, `ACL`, `BIND`, `CHECKOUT`, `COPY`, `LINK`, `LOCK`, `M-SEARCH`, `MERGE`, `MKACTIVITY`, `MKCALENDAR`, `MKCOL`, `MOVE`, `NOTIFY`, `PROPFIND`, `PROPPATCH`, `PURGE`, `REBIND`, `REPORT`, `SEARCH`, `SOURCE`, `SUBSCRIBE`, `UNBIND`, `UNLINK`, `UNLOCK` and `UNSUBSCRIBE`. Each may carry a body. A `QUERY` without a `Content-Type`, or with one but no body, is captured like the same request sent with `POST`.

**Path.** `/s/{sessionId}`, `/s/{sessionId}/` and any path under it — `/s/{sessionId}/stripe/events`, `/s/{sessionId}/folder/` — are one endpoint, captured and answered exactly the same way unless the session's response rules answer the method and the path; OpenAPI has no way to write a path of any depth, so only the first is listed. The path a request was sent to is stored exactly as sent — dot segments, doubled slashes and percent-encoding intact — and returned as `path` by `GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}/requests/{requestId}`; the query string is stored apart from it. The segment after `/s/` alone is the session: an unknown one, or one that cannot be an id, answers `404` / `1001 SESSION_NOT_FOUND` whatever path follows it, and stores nothing.

**Headers, version and address.** Every request header is stored exactly as the sender wrote it: its name in the sender's case, in the sender's order, duplicates included, and nothing is added. The webhook host speaks HTTP/1.1 alone, so an HTTP/2 client falls back to it and the request is stored with `httpVersion` `1.1`. The sender's address is the one its connection came from; a sender's own `X-Forwarded-For` or `X-Real-Ip` is stored as a header and changes nothing.

**Default and custom sessions.** A default session answers `200` with `{ "ok": true, "requestId": "<uuid>", … }`: the id of the stored request, `message` (`Captured by QA Tools`, `Captured by Webhook Inspector` from the date the changelog's 1.19.0 entry gives), `inspectorUrl` — the request on its session's page, `https://qa-tools.ru/v/{sessionId}#<uuid>` — and the stored `receivedAt`, `method`, `path`, `bodySize` and `sourceIp`; nothing of the request's body, headers or query string. A custom session answers with its configured status, headers, body and delay. A session with response rules answers a request whose method and path match one with the first such rule's response, before anything else, and records the rule; the path matched is what follows `/s/{sessionId}`, exactly as sent, without the query. A session with a response queue answers every other request with the queue's next step first, whichever its response, and records the step it took. The delay is waited out after the request is stored and shown, so the inspector shows the request while the sender is still waiting. An error response is never delayed and never carries the configured headers.

**Headers on the answer.** Every stored request is answered with `X-Webhook-Inspector-Request-Id: <uuid>`, the id of the stored request, usable with `GET /api/sessions/{sessionId}/requests/{requestId}`, and with the same id in `X-QA-Tools-Request-Id`, its old name, until the date the changelog's 1.19.0 entry gives.
